The area was Doggerland, a landmass now beneath the southern North Sea. It stretched from Britain's east coast to the Netherlands, the western coasts of Germany and the Jutland peninsula, and it was probably a rich habitat with Mesolithic human habitation.

Rising sea levels flooded it around 6,500–6,200 BCE, gradually reducing it to low-lying islands. Its final submergence was possibly caused by a tsunami from the Storegga Slide. This underwater landslide occurred at the edge of Norway's continental shelf around 6225–6170 BCE. It involved about 290 km of coastal shelf and roughly 3,500 km³ of debris, and it generated a very large tsunami in the North Atlantic Ocean.

The submergence was driven mainly by rising sea levels, and the tsunami was probably only the final blow.

title: Doggerland

Doggerland was an area now beneath the southern North Sea that connected Great Britain to continental Europe during and after the last glacial period. It was flooded by rising sea levels around 6,500–6,200 BCE. Geological surveys have suggested that it stretched from Britain's east coast to the Netherlands and the western coasts of Germany and the peninsula of Jutland. It was probably a rich habitat with human habitation in the Mesolithic period, although rising sea levels gradually reduced it to low-lying islands before its final submergence, possibly following a tsunami caused by the Storegga Slide.

title: Storegga Slide

The three Storegga Slides are considered to be amongst the largest known landslides. They occurred under water, at the edge of Norway's continental shelf in the Norwegian Sea, approximately 6225–6170 BCE. The collapse involved an estimated 290 km length of coastal shelf, with a total volume of 3500 km3 of debris, which caused a very large tsunami in the North Atlantic Ocean.
